heading: 5 Discussion and conclusion
text: Several practical lessons follow from these results. Multimodality by itself is not a sufficient description of optimization difficulty: a landscape may contain many local minima without making local optimization particularly costly if those minima have similar objective values, in which case independent restarts can provide effective exploration. The situation changes when local optimization terminates in basins with substantially different objective values, because missing a good basin then becomes costly and broader exploration can be useful even under a function-evaluation-matched multistart baseline. This distinction explains the MaxCut results, where increasing independent depth mainly increases sampled local structure, whereas parameter tying also produces a much larger spread in local-search endpoint quality.

heading: 5 Discussion and conclusion
text: Although the optimizer sees E(θ) simply as a real-valued classical function, its geometry is induced jointly by the Hamiltonian, the reachable quantum states, and their parameterization. Different geometric descriptions should therefore not be conflated: the pullback/Fubini-Study metric measures sensitivity of the represented state to parameter motion, the Hessian describes local curvature of the scalar objective, and random-start endpoint statistics measure how reliably local optimization reaches good or poor basins. In the examples considered here, these endpoint statistics are more directly connected to the local-versus-global optimizer comparison than local curvature alone. Conversely, the way a population method proposes new points is an algorithm-side property rather than a property of the objective itself; proposal geometry for SOMA and differential evolution is studied separately in Ref..

heading: 5 Discussion and conclusion
text: Parameter tying provides a particularly simple example of how the optimizer coordinates can matter as much as their number. Sharing parameters is also common in machine learning, for example in recurrent or shared-depth architectures, where it can improve parameter efficiency or impose useful inductive structure. The analogy here is limited to the optimization mechanism: reusing one variable at several stages of a nonlinear computation couples the effect of that variable across those stages. In the tied QAOA construction, the classical search dimension remains D = 6, but each angle controls several physical circuit layers. The resulting problem is therefore lower-dimensional than an independently parameterized circuit of the same physical depth, but it is not necessarily easier to optimize. Parameter count alone is consequently a poor proxy for optimization difficulty.

heading: 5 Discussion and conclusion
text: An important limitation of the present experiments is that all objective values are obtained from exact statevector simulations. The optimizer therefore sees a deterministic expectation value rather than an estimate constructed from a finite number of quantum measurements. On actual quantum hardware, even an otherwise ideal circuit produces sampling noise because ⟨H⟩ must be estimated from finitely many measurement shots. This distinction can matter substantially for optimizer behavior. Quasi-Newton methods such as BFGS rely on sufficiently consistent local changes in the objective to construct gradient and curvature information and to perform line searches. Noisy objective differences can therefore make these steps unreliable. Derivative-free population methods such as differential evolution do not require local gradient estimates and are often more tolerant of stochastic objective evaluations, although noise can still degrade their selection and increase the required evaluation budget. Optimization under noisy VQA objectives is studied separately in Ref.. The relative performance observed here for exact objectives should therefore not be assumed to remain quantitatively unchanged under finite-shot sampling.

heading: 5 Discussion and conclusion
text: Finite sampling is also distinct from quantum-hardware noise. Gate errors, decoherence, calibration errors, and readout noise can change the objective itself in addition to making its estimate uncertain; these effects are outside the scope of the present study. Likewise, the examples considered here did not exhibit an apparent barren-plateau regime: the optimization difficulty studied in this paper comes from local-minimum and basin structure rather than from an observed collapse of gradient magnitudes. Barren plateaus are a separate trainability mechanism and may become important for different ansatzes, depths, or system sizes.

heading: 5 Discussion and conclusion
text: The visualizations in this paper are intended to answer specific optimization questions rather than to summarize the objective with a single geometric picture. Coordinate and optimizer-informed slices are exact restrictions of the objective along selected directions, while basin embeddings use constructed coordinates to show relationships among sampled minima; likewise, minima counted along one-dimensional probes measure directional multimodality rather than the total number of minima. These views are therefore most useful when interpreted together with random-start endpoint statistics. The optimizer comparison should be read with the same scope in mind: it uses small exactly simulated instances, fixed function-evaluation budgets, and best-observed rather than certified global optima, so it is a controlled comparison rather than a universal optimizer ranking. Within these experiments, the main distinction is that increasing sampled local structure alone does not imply an advantage for global evolutionary search; what matters more is whether local optimization repeatedly reaches solutions of similar quality or becomes trapped in substantially worse basins. This reflects the broader point that Hamiltonian choice, circuit construction, and parameterization determine not only which states are reachable, but also the classical optimization problem presented to the optimizer.

text:
The following figures in this appendix provide three complementary controls: analytically constructed objectives that calibrate the visual vocabulary, spin-glassinspired scans that isolate parameter tying, and molecular VHA scans that show that compact parameterizations can remain smooth. Analytic and classical controls. Figure 11 provides a deliberately simple calibration case. The Fourier objectives contain several local wells while remaining fully controlled two-parameter functions, so they show the difference between many local minima and unequal local-minimum quality without any quantummodel details. The Rastrigin- and Schwefel-like panels connect that distinction to familiar global-optimization examples.

heading: A Additional examples and controls
text:
Molecular VHA controls. The molecular examples in Fig. 13 provide an important counterexample to any simple rule that parameter tying or low dimension must produce a difficult objective function. Several of the H2 and H4 VHA scans remain smooth or contain only a few sampled minima even as the parameterization changes. These examples show that optimization difficulty depends jointly on the physical model, ansatz, and parameterization.

Taken together, the appendix galleries support the same interpretation used in the main text. Repeated structure can be introduced by construction, and its optimization consequence is model dependent. Useful diagnostics therefore include both a measure of sampled local-minimum density and measures of the quality and accessibility of solutions reached by local search.

heading: Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (MQE): A Selective State Space Model for Scalable Ground State Simulations in Quantum Chemistry
heading_path: Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (MQE): A Selective State Space Model for Scalable Ground State Simulations in Quantum Chemistry
text: Predicting molecular electronic structure using Quantum Computing approaches is a challenge in Computational Chemistry. Traditional Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQEs) are typically hindered by optimization challenges. The alternative Generative Quantum Eigensolver (GQE) mitigates this by reformulating ground-state search as discrete sequence generation, but its Transformer backbone suffers from quadratic computational complexity, bottlenecking scalability for larger molecules. To address this, we introduce the Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (Mamba-QE), which replaces the Transformer with a Selective State Space Model (SSM) to process operator sequences with linear O(L) complexity. Additionally, we integrate a distance-conditioned mechanism enabling the direct prediction of complete potential energy surfaces (PES). Evaluated on the H2 molecule, Mamba-QE reproduces Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) reference energies well within chemical accuracy, achieving an energy error below 3 × 10-6 Ha across 16 geometries with zero variational violations. Mamba-QE maintains high expressive power while establishing a robust, scalable foundation for quantum simulations of complex molecular systems.

heading: I. INTRODUCTION
text: Predicting the electronic structure of molecules is a fundamental challenge in computational chemistry, with direct implications for catalyst design, materials discovery, and pharmaceutical development. Solving the electronic Schr¨odinger equation exactly is resource-demanding for most systems. Consequently, approximate methods have been developed, balancing computational cost against chemical accuracy. Nevertheless, many chemically relevant systems, particularly those with strong electron correlation, remain beyond scalable classical approximations, motivating the development of quantum algorithms that exploit quantum hardware to accelerate molecular simulations.

heading: I. INTRODUCTION
text: Among the most promising approaches for near-term quantum devices are Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs), particularly the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE). This approach combines parameterized quantum circuits with a classical optimization loop to estimate molecular ground-state energies through the variational principle. The framework has demonstrated success for small molecules and has become one of the most extensively studied quantum algorithms for electronic structure calculations. However, its scalability is limited by well-known challenges, including barren plateaus, optimization instability, strong dependence on ansatz design, and the increasing computational cost of the hybrid optimization loop as circuit depth and molecular complexity grow. These limitations motivate the search for alternatives that reduce or eliminate continuous parameter optimization.

heading: I. INTRODUCTION
text:
A recent approach in this direction is the Generative Quantum Eigensolver (GQE), which reformulates ground-state search as a generative sequence modeling problem. Instead of optimizing continuous parameters within a fixed quantum circuit, GQE trains a generative model to construct quantum circuits by sequentially selecting operators from a predefined gate pool. The generated circuits are evaluated on a quantum processor, and their measured energies are used as reward signals for reinforcement learning. By transferring the optimization process from a continuous parameter landscape to a discrete sequence generation task, GQE searches to reduce the barren plateau while enabling adaptive circuit discovery.

The original GQE employs a Transformer architecture inspired by GPT models as its generative backbone. However, the self-attention mechanism in this architecture exhibits quadratic computational and memory complexity with respect to sequence length. As molecular systems become larger, longer operator sequences are required to represent quantum circuits, causing the computational cost of the Transformer backbone to grow rapidly. Consequently, the scalability of the classical sequence model itself becomes a bottleneck for extending GQE to larger molecular systems.

heading: I. INTRODUCTION
text:
This motivates exploring alternative architectures that preserve the expressive power of Transformers while offering lower computational complexity. Recently, Selective State Space Models (SSMs), particularly the Mamba architecture, have emerged as a promising alternative. Rather than relying on self-attention, Mamba employs an input-dependent state-space formulation that processes sequences with linear computational complexity while maintaining competitive modeling capability across a broad range of sequence learning tasks.

Building directly upon the GQE framework, we propose the Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (Mamba-QE). Architecturally, Mamba-QE is a targeted enhancement of the GQE paradigm: it replaces the O(L2 ) multi-head self-attention backbone of GPTQE with a Mamba-based SSM, effectively scaling the sequence processing engine to linear O(L) complexity while preserving the core discrete-optimization reinforcement learning loop.

heading: I. INTRODUCTION
text:
Leveraging this efficient linear-complexity backbone, we further extend GQE by introducing a continuous distance-conditioning mechanism, ϕ(R). While previous GQE implementations require training independent models for isolated molecular geometries, our geometric embedding concatenates interatomic spatial coordinates directly into the token representations. This allows a single unified Mamba-QE policy to generate tailored quantum circuits across an entire Potential Energy Surface (PES), transforming GQE from a static point-wise solver into a geometrically continuous generative framework.

From a chemical perspective, traditional physicsinspired ans¨atze, such as Unitary Coupled Cluster with Singles and Doubles (UCCSD), offer rigor but scale steeply in circuit depth (O(N 4 ) or higher in terms of spinorbitals). While generative frameworks mitigate this by sampling compact, problem-tailored operator sequences, Transformer-based backbones quickly hit an O(L2 ) computational bottleneck as the required sequence length L grows for larger active spaces and strongly correlated regimes.

heading: I. INTRODUCTION
text:
By replacing the Transformer with a SSMs, MambaQE eliminates this bottleneck, maintaining linear O(L) scaling. This efficiency is essential for scaling generative circuit discovery to complex chemical phenomena, such as transition-metal complexes, bond-breaking processes, and open-shell radicals, where capturing both static and dynamic correlation demands longer operator sequences and standard VQE optimizations collapse into barren plateaus.

Furthermore, analyzing the operator sequences generated by Mamba-QE provides direct physical interpretability. By tracking which quantum gates the model prioritizes across different geometries, one can map the onset of dynamic versus static correlation along a PES. Thus, Mamba-QE serves not only as a scalable solver for ground-state energies but also as a generative tool for deciphering the essential correlation structures of complex chemical systems.

heading: I. INTRODUCTION
text:
As a proof-of-concept validation of this methodology, the proposed architecture is evaluated on the hydrogen molecule (H2), where it reproduces Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) reference energies, achieving an energy error below 3 × 10-6 Ha across 16 internuclear distances with zero variational violations. While benchmarks on H2 do not yet expose hardware scaling limits, they establish the foundational empirical evidence that transitioning to a linear-complexity SSM retains high physical expressivity without degrading optimization stability, providing a scalable backbone for deeper quantum circuits in complex chemical systems.

Taken together, these developments establish MambaQE as a generative framework that connects efficient sequence modeling with geometry-aware quantum circuit generation for molecular electronic-structure calculations. The H2 results provide a proof of concept for this approach and establish a basis for investigating its scalability to larger molecular systems.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the methodology, including the Generative Quantum Eigensolver framework, the Mambabased architecture, the distance-conditioning mechanism, and the dynamic quality-threshold scheduling. Section III presents and discusses the numerical results for H2. Finally, Section IV summarizes the main findings and discusses directions for future work.

heading: A. Generative Quantum Eigensolver and the GPT-QE Baseline
heading_path: A. Generative Quantum Eigensolver and the GPT-QE Baseline
text:
The Generative Quantum Eigensolver (GQE) is a hybrid quantum-classical framework that recasts groundstate search as a discrete optimization problem solved via generative modeling. Rather than optimizing the continuous parameters of a fixed ansatz circuit, as in VQE, GQE trains a classical generative model to sample sequences of operators from a predefined gate pool P = {U1, U2,..., UK}. The generative model therefore produces an ordered sequence of operator indices, ⃗j = (j1,..., jL), which is then mapped to a quantum circuit by composing the corresponding operators,

is applied to a reference state |ρ0⟩ to yield trial states whose energy expectation values serve as a reward signal during training. This formulation shifts the search from the highly non-convex continuous optimization of circuit parameters to the discrete space of circuit architectures.

The original implementation proposed by Nakaji et al. employs a decoder-only Transformer architecture, specifically a GPT-2-style model as the generative backbone, giving rise to the GPT-QE baseline. In GPT-QE, the generative model is trained autoregressively: at each step t, it computes a conditional probability distribution pθ(jt | j1,..., jt-1) over the operator pool and samples the next gate. The sequence probability factorizes as

where L denotes the sequence length. The model parameters θ are updated via a reinforcement learning objective using the expectation value ⟨Ψ(⃗j)| ˆH|Ψ(⃗j)⟩ as the cost function to minimize. The self-attention mechanism of the Transformer, operating with O(L2 ) computational and memory complexity in the sequence length L, captures long-range dependencies between previously selected gates to inform future selections.

Despite the success of this approach in demonstrating the feasibility of generative circuit search for molecular electronic structure Hamiltonians, the quadratic scaling of the Transformer attention mechanism presents a bottleneck as the operator sequence length, and thus the circuit depth, grows with system size. For molecules requiring large active spaces, such sequences can become prohibitively long, making the computational cost of GPT-QE training a limiting factor for practical applications.

heading: B. Mamba-QE: A Selective State Space Model Alternative
heading_path: B. Mamba-QE: A Selective State Space Model Alternative
text:
To address the scalability limitations of the Transformer backbone, we propose replacing the GPT architecture in GQE with the Mamba architecture, yielding the Mamba-QE framework. Mamba is a selective state space model (SSM) that processes sequences with linear complexity O(L) in the sequence length while retaining competitive modeling capacity relative to Transformers. The key innovation of Mamba over earlier SSMs such as S4 is the introduction of input-dependent, content-aware gating: the parameters (B, C, ∆) are parameterized as functions of the current input, enabling the model to selectively propagate or discard information along the sequence at a substantially lower computational cost than multi-head self-attention.

This selectivity allows Mamba to model long-range dependencies in operator sequences without the quadratic memory overhead of self-attention, enabling hardware-aware parallel training via a associative scan algorithm while retaining an O(1) state memory overhead per step during autoregressive generation.

After the warm-up stage, Mamba-QE enters an iterative refinement phase. At predefined refinement iterations, the current model generates candidate operator sequences conditioned on randomly selected molecular geometries. Each generated sequence is evaluated with the quantum simulator, and its final energy is used to determine whether the sequence is admitted to the replay buffer. The buffer therefore converts quantum evaluations into additional supervised training data.

At each subsequent training iteration, the model is trained using a mixture of the original randomly generated dataset and samples drawn from the replay buffer. In the present implementation, the default buffer contribution during refinement is 30% of each training batch, while the warm-up phase uses no replay-buffer samples. This procedure progressively shifts part of the training distribution toward lower-energy circuits while retaining randomly generated examples to preserve exploration.

heading: III. RESULTS AND DISCUSION
text:
The proposed Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (MambaQE) was evaluated on the hydrogen molecule (H2), considering the prediction of the complete potential energy surface (PES) across 16 interatomic distances. Table II summarizes the quantitative results obtained by the model.

The proposed architecture successfully reproduces the Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) reference energies with remarkable accuracy. The minimum energy predicted by Mamba-QE is -1.136186 Ha, differing from the exact FCI minimum of -1.136189 Ha by less than 3 × 10-6 Ha, which corresponds to an error well below the chemical accuracy threshold of 1 kcal/mol (approximately 1.6 mHa). Moreover, chemical accuracy was achieved for all 16 molecular geometries evaluated, demonstrating that the proposed architecture generalizes consistently across the entire potential energy surface rather than only around the equilibrium geometry.

An important observation is that no variational violations were detected during the optimization process. Since the variational principle guarantees that approximate energies should not fall below the exact groundstate energy, the absence of violations indicates that the reinforcement learning procedure remained numerically stable while preserving the physical consistency of the generated quantum circuits.

The replay buffer statistics further illustrate the learning dynamics of the generative model. Although the mean energy stored in the final buffer (-1.006522 Ha)

remains significantly above the ground-state energy, the best circuit found reaches -1.134656 Ha before the final refinement stage. This behavior suggests that the policy explores a diverse set of candidate circuits while progressively concentrating probability mass around lowerenergy solutions. Such diversity is particularly desirable in reinforcement learning settings, preventing premature convergence to suboptimal circuit structures.

Unlike GPT-QE, whose Transformer backbone requires quadratic computational complexity with respect to the circuit length, the proposed Mamba-QE replaces the attention mechanism with a selective state-space model exhibiting linear complexity. Although the H2 benchmark is too small to expose significant runtime differences, these results validate that replacing the Transformer does not degrade predictive accuracy. Therefore, the experimental evidence supports the hypothesis that Mamba-QE preserves the optimization capability of generative quantum eigensolvers while offering a substantially more scalable sequence modeling architecture for deeper quantum circuits and larger molecular systems.

heading: IV. CONCLUSION
text:
In this work, we introduced the Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (Mamba-QE), a generative framework for ground-state molecular simulation that replaces the quadratic-complexity Transformer backbone of GPT-QE with a Selective State Space Model (SSM) exhibiting linear complexity with respect to sequence length. Furthermore, by incorporating a distance-conditioning mechanism, ϕ(R), Mamba-QE extends the Generative Quantum Eigensolver (GQE) paradigm from single-geometry optimization to the direct generation of quantum circuits across an entire potential energy surface (PES) within a single, unified policy.

Evaluated on the H2 molecule, Mamba-QE reproduced Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) reference energies with chemical accuracy across all 16 sampled internuclear distances. The model achieved a minimum-energy error below 3 × 10-6Ha and maintained zero variational violations throughout training. These results confirm that substituting the attention mechanism with a selective SSM preserves both the expressive power and the optimization stability of the generative approach, while successfully eliminating the O(L2 ) scaling bottleneck that restricts Transformer-based GQE implementations as circuit depth and active-space sizes increase.

heading: IV. CONCLUSION
text: Although the H2 benchmark rigorously validates the methodology and establishes a robust proof of concept, larger molecular systems are required to fully expose the runtime advantages inherent to the linearcomplexity backbone. Future work will therefore extend Mamba-QE to larger, strongly correlated systems-such as transition-metal complexes and complex bond-breaking regimes-to directly quantify runtime scaling relative to GPT-QE. Additionally, we aim to investigate whether the distance-conditioning mechanism generalizes to multi-dimensional geometric parameter spaces beyond a single internuclear coordinate. Further research directions include exploring transfer learning across diverse molecular configurations, integrating the framework with hardware-executed circuit evaluations, and conducting deeper interpretability analyses of the operator sequences selected by the model to disentangle static and dynamic electronic correlation along the PES.

heading: Abstract
text:
Quantum computing is a rapidly developed field of science. In the NISC era, quantum machine learning stands out, potentially outperforming classical machine learning. In this paper, we explore the applicability of quantum machine learning to a real-world application. We solved the problem of prediction of the temperature of GPUs in a high-performance computing cluster. We trained a quantum circuit to predict the temperature of each of the eight GPU of each cluster node based on 16 physical parameters. We demonstrated that quantum machine learning performs on this task just as well as classical machine learning. Furthermore, using model problems, we demonstrated that quantum machine learning can potentially outperform classical machine learning.

Keywords: QML, quantum machine learning, practical task, prediction analytics

heading: 1 Introduction
text:
In the modern era of digital transformation, predictive analytics is becoming a key tool for improving operational efficiency across various industries. One of the most important practical applications in this area is predictive maintenance, which enables the prediction of equipment failures and optimization of repair schedules, significantly reducing downtime and operating costs. The implementation of predictive analytics enables more precise prediction of equipment failures, thereby reducing operating costs and downtime.

Machine learning (ML) methods, including deep learning methods, are traditionally used to solve predictive maintenance problems. These methods analyze historical data from equipment sensors, identify hidden patterns, and generate predictions of probable failures. However, with increasing data complexity and dimensionality, traditional ML methods encounter computational limitations, stimulating the search for more powerful computing paradigms.

Concurrent with the development of classical ML, rapid progress is occurring in quantum computing - a technology based on principles of quantum mechanics such as superposition and entanglement. The use of qubits (quantum bits) instead of classical bits opens up the possibility of exponential growth in computing power for certain classes of problems.

heading: 1 Introduction
text:
Quantum Machine Learning (QML) is a rapidly developing interdisciplinary field at the intersection of quantum computing and machine learning. QML explores how quantum computers can improve or accelerate traditional ML algorithms. The underlying hypothesis is that quantum computers are capable of working with much more complex and high-dimensional feature spaces due to their fundamental properties. Access to these extended Hilbert spaces allows to create the kernel functions that are extremely difficult or impossible to reproduce on classical machines, opening the way to solving problems previously considered computationally intractable.

In recent years, a number of scientific papers have appeared demonstrating the potential effectiveness of qubits in machine learning. Useful properties include nonlinearity, the use of gradient descent and gradient calculation using the parameter-shift rule, and the demonstration of good results on simple problems. Furthermore, such factors as the exponential growth of the dimension of the Hilbert space, quantum entanglement, and the unitarity of algorithms support the effectiveness of quantum machine learning.

heading: 1 Introduction
text:
Experiments on benchmark datasets (such as MNIST datasets) show that hybrid models can achieve competitive or even superior accuracy compared to fully classical machine learning algorithms while simultaneously reducing the number of parameters. This supports the thesis that quantum circuits are capable of implementing highly expressive and nonlinear transformations that effective for classification and regression problems. Moreover even one qubit can tackle the challenge of classification and regression.

Despite encouraging results, a significant drawback of the most existing works in QML area are focus on simplified model problems (toy problems) and benchmark datasets of limited size. Typically, demonstrations of a "quantum advantage" are limited to general statements about the fundamental properties of quantum systems-superposition, entanglement, and Hilbert space operation-without a deep investigation of the nature of this advantage or the identification of specific types of problems or data dependencies where QML is most effective. The lack of systematic research aimed at identifying such dependencies, as well as the application of QML to real industrial problems with large volumes of data (big data), hinders the transition from laboratory experiments to field implementation.

The aim of this study is to apply quantum machine learning to a practical predictive maintenance problem using a large dataset of real equipment telemetry data, as well as to

heading: 1 Introduction
text:
systematically investigate the potential advantages of QML over classical neural networks.

To achieve this goal we completed the following set of tasks:

Conducting a series of experiments with parameterized quantum circuits on regression problems using model functions to identify the types of dependencies and data characteristics for which QML consistently demonstrates better accuracy than classical neural networks.

Selection of the optimal quantum circuit architecture based on a competetive analysis, with demonstrating of the highest efficiency for the identified classes of dependencies.

Testing of the best selected QML architecture on a real-world predictive maintenance problem with a large dataset containing industrial equipment telemetry data.

This two-step approach allows us not only to propose a potentially more efficient solution for a specific application problem, but also to contribute to the fundamental understanding of the applicability of quantum machine learning by moving from general statements to quantitatively substantiated conclusions. We used simulator of quantum computer for modeling quantum circuit. Calculations are carried out without taking into account the noise.

heading: 3 Task Description. Dataset
text:
This work addressed the problem of predictive analytics for high-performance servers with GPU that used in HPC clusters for parallel computations.

The node servers are the DGX A100 servers from NVidia, which includes:

Telemetry data is collected via the BMC port. Each server has its own built-in mechanism for managing server operating parameters. Specifically, when the server's operating temperature rises to a threshold of 80 degrees Celsius, the server's automation increases the fan rotation speed to enhance cooling, and when the threshold temperature is exceeded, it reduces power consumption and server performance. The exact algorithms of the server's automation are unknown, but thanks to them, the server maintains operation even with significant performance losses and cooling disruptions. The server's automation does not notify administrators of these operating modes. Entering this mode of operation, among other things, reduces the performance of the HPC cluster when performing parallel calculations. Figure 1 shows a blower diagram of the DGX A100 GPU server.

heading: 4 QML Model
text:
The application of quantum machine learning methods requires the selection of a quantum circuit architecture that optimizes the cost of computing resources for model training and resources during operation, subject to achieving the target performance.

We based our design on the quantum circuit architecture from, which considers three types of quantum circuits for QML: a simple quantum circuit, a quantum kernel, and a reuploading circuit. An example of a 4-qubit circuit is shown in Figure 2. The quantum circuit of their N qubits consists of an input layer, ansatz layers, and a measurement layer. The input layer consists of rotation gates Rx(θin i ) located on each qubit, i.e., i = 1,... N. The ansatz plays the role of a learning layer and consists of NL identical layers. Each layer contains rotation gates at three angles:

where i is the qubit number, j is the layer number. The layers contains N control NOT (CNOT) entanglement gates, as shown in the figure. The set and arrangement of gates are identical in each layer. The output of the measurement layer is the average value of each qubit. Since we obtain the data using a quantum computer simulator, there is no need to perform the measurement multiple times and then average it. We use the average value of the gate operator Z obtained from the wave function mi = ⟨ψ∗ |Zi| ψ⟩.

heading: 4 QML Model
text:
Figure 2: Example of 4 qubits quantum scheme with 3 ansatz layers. It consists of the input layer, few layers of ansatz and the measurement layer. Every ansatz layer consists of rotation gates and entanglement gates. It can include re-uploading gates. Attritionary the scheme includes linear layers on the input and output in order to scaling functions.

Additionally, before each ansatz layer, one additional rotator Rx(θin 1 ) can be included with a rotation angle equal to the rotation angle on the zero qubit of the input layer and acting on the first qubit. This scheme is called re-uploading. A scheme without additional rotators in the ansatz will be called a simple quantum circuit.

text:
The most important result of the study is the confirmation of the ability of quantum circuits to solve real-world practical problems. Also we obtaine new theoretical results.

The computational experiments confirmed the following patterns:

Quantum machine learning algorithms enable to traine the regression models for predicting of the values of complex functions describing various physical processes,

They enable the modeling of various patterns described by combinations of periodic, decaying, polynomial, and step functions,

They are preferred for modeling periodic and decaying processes. Furthermore, a quantum circuit perfectly approximates a fully harmonic function (e.g., y = sin(x)) - the mean deviation is MAD = 0.

However, quantum circuits with different architectures show different results, and the reuploading scheme has better performance over a simple quantum circuit. The re-uploading scheme is similar to the residual connection technique in neural networks. Possibly that the quantum circuits have the ability to forget signals like multilayer neural networks. This point should be the subject of further research.

heading: 7 Discussion
text:
By using an expression metric (the network's ability to approximate complex functions with the fixed number of parameters) for comparing of the performance of networks of different architectures, we observed the effect that predicted by the universal approximation theorem. Specifically, prediction accuracy increases with increasing number of qubits and layers.

Furthermore, the increase of prediction accuracy as result of increasing the number of layers in the quantum circuit confirms that the quantum circuit itself provides the primary contribution to accurate prediction, with the input and output layers acting as feature layers.

Despite of telemetry data noising caused by acting of the server fan control system and thermal hysteresis, the model predicts server temperatures for given power consumption and utilization with accuracy that sufficient for server overheating detection as a result of fans and control system failures.

heading: 7 Discussion
text:
The average deviation of the predicted temperature was MAD = 1.41◦C with maximum deviation around 15◦C. However, the histogram in Figure 21 shows that an error greater than 5◦C is extremely rare. Based on these points we consider a measured temperature exceeding the predicted temperature by 4◦C as a signal of hardware failure.

In the next steps, we plan to study the performance of quantum circuits taking into account the quantum noise, as well as examine the temperature prediction capabilities of both approaches depending on the dataset size and the ability of overfitting of the quantum circuit.

A practical problem solution showed that the neural network slightly outperformed the results of the quantum circuit (Figure 23). This may be due, among other things, to the fact that the server temperature depends on the active influence of the server management system and fan operation, including possible stepwise switching between different operating modes. Further research should clarify the range of conditions under which quantum circuits and quantum machine learning algorithms can effectively implement quantum supremacy.

heading: 8 Conclusions
text: In our work, we demonstrated that the quantum circuit is capable of solving the practical problem of server temperature prediction, as well as a range of other regression tasks. All computations were performed on a quantum device simulator. The results show that this approach to solving practical problems can be implemented on a real quantum computer.

heading: A Quantum Algorithm for Computing All Eigenvalues and Eigenstates of Sparse Hermitian Matrices
heading_path: A Quantum Algorithm for Computing All Eigenvalues and Eigenstates of Sparse Hermitian Matrices

* Cryptology and Security Research Unit, Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata, India † Electronics and Communication Sciences Unit, Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata, India

heading: Abstract
text: Computation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a sparse Hermitian matrix is a fundamental problem in algebra, arising both as a problem of independent interest and as a key subroutine in a wide range of computational and scientific applications. In this work, we develop a quantum algorithm that determines the spectrum of a sparse Hermitian matrix, defined as the set of its distinct eigenvalues, and for each eigenvalue, prepares a corresponding eigenvector as a quantum state in its eigenspace. The eigenvalues are represented as binary strings with a prescribed precision, while the corresponding eigenvectors are kept as quantum states, eliminating the need to reconstruct their classical counterparts. The algorithm instead enables estimation of expectation values ⟨x|M|x⟩, where |x⟩ is a prepared eigenstate and M is an observable. For an n × n s-sparse Hermitian matrix H, dense methods based on Householder tridiagonalization and QR iteration compute all eigenvalues and eigenvectors in O(n3 ) time. Exploiting sparsity, the Lanczos method computes all eigenvalues in O(n2 s) time in exact arithmetic, but recovering all eigenvectors still requires O(n3 ) time. In contrast, our algorithm runs in time ˜O(ns2 log 2 n/∆min), where ∆min denotes the minimum spectral gap of the normalized matrix. For inverse gaps up to ∆-1 min = O(n), the most favorable scaling for n distinct eigenvalues, attained by nearly uniformly spaced spectra such as those of perfect-state-transfer spin chains and the

heading: Abstract
text: favorable scaling for n distinct eigenvalues, attained by nearly uniformly spaced spectra such as those of perfect-state-transfer spin chains and the Sylvester-Kac matrix, and for sparsity up to s = o(√n/ log n), the proposed algorithm achieves an improved asymptotic runtime over the classical O(n3 ) approach for computing all eigenvalues and eigenvectors, under standard sparse-access assumptions.

heading: 1 Introduction
text:
This spectral information associated with a matrix plays an important role in various areas of computer science, including graph analysis and combinatorial optimization. A wellknown classical method for computing the spectrum of a dense matrix is the tridiagonal QR algorithm. It first reduces a matrix to tridiagonal form using Householder reflections, requiring approximately 4 3 n3 floating-point operations (flops) for a real symmetric matrix. Once the matrix is reduced to tridiagonal form, all of its eigenvalues can be computed using the implicitly shifted QR algorithm in O(n2 ) operations. Therefore, the overall computational complexity remains O(n3 ), dominated by the tridiagonalization step. For an n×n s-sparse Hermitian matrix, the Lanczos algorithm computes all eigenvalues in O(n2s) operations in exact arithmetic: n iterations of O(ns)

sparse matrix-vector products, followed by an O(n2 ) tridiagonal eigensolve. Recovering all n eigenvectors additionally requires storing the Lanczos basis Q and forming X = QY, where Y holds the tridiagonal eigenvectors, obtainable in O(n2 ) time via MRRR. This dense product costs O(n3 ) operations, or O(nω ) with fast matrix multiplication, where ω < 2.372. In floating point, the Lanczos vectors lose orthogonality as Ritz values converge, so full reorthogonalization, at an additional O(n3 ) cost, is needed for an accurate, orthogonal set of eigenvectors.

heading: 1 Introduction
text: Two major components of quantum computing are qubits and quantum gates that are analogous to classical bits and classical gates, respectively. Quantum computing has the potential to provide advantages for certain classical computational tasks by exploiting fundamental quantum-mechanical properties, such as superposition and entanglement. Superposition allows a quantum state to be represented as a linear combination of tensor products of qubits, while entanglement enables correlations between qubits that have no direct classical counterpart. These properties enable the development of quantum algorithms that can address certain computational problems more efficiently than their classical counterparts, particularly in areas such as optimization, simulation, and numerical linear algebra. Current quantum computing platforms are characterized by the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era, featuring increasingly capable quantum devices with more qubits and improved computational reliability.

heading: 1 Introduction
text: In this work, we present a quantum algorithm for determining the spectrum of a sparse Hermitian matrix H, together with the corresponding eigenvectors. We focus specifically on reconstructing the distinct spectrum of the Hamiltonian, defined as the set of unique eigenvalues spec(H) = {λ1,..., λd}, where d ≤ n. When an eigenvalue λj is degenerate (appearing with multiplicity mj > 1), measuring an estimated eigenvalue within its tolerance bin collapses the state register into the corresponding eigenvector space Vλj = span{|x⟩ | H|x⟩ = λj|x⟩}. The eigenvalues are obtained in classical binary-string form with a prescribed precision, providing an explicit classical representation of the spectrum. In contrast, the corresponding eigenvectors are maintained in quantum-state form, rather than being explicitly reconstructed as classical vectors. Instead, relevant properties of the corresponding eigenvectors can be characterized by directly estimating expectation values of observables of the form ⟨x|M|x⟩, where |x⟩ denotes the quantum state corresponding to an eigenvector and M is a given observable. Our algorithm is based on the Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) algorithm and consists of three main stages. First, the given sparse Hermitian matrix is mapped to a corresponding unitary operator suitable for phase estimation. Second, QPE is applied to this unitary operator multiple times, with a predefined computational basis state used as the input state of the eigenvector register in each

heading: 1 Introduction
text: to this unitary operator multiple times, with a predefined computational basis state used as the input state of the eigenvector register in each execution. Finally, in each execution, the eigenvalue register is measured to obtain the corresponding eigenvalue in classical binary-string form. At the same time, the associated eigenvector is retained as a quantum state in the eigenvector register. The overall runtime of the proposed algorithm is ˜O ( ns2 log 2 (n) ∆min ), where ∆min denotes the minimum spectral gap. For inverse minimum spectral gaps up to ∆-1 min = O(n), and under the stated sparsity and matrix-access assumptions, this complexity yields an improved asymptotic scaling compared with the O(n3 ) runtime of conventional classical methods for computing eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Such spectra arise, for example, in spin chains engineered for perfect quantum state transfer, whose single-excitation Hamiltonians have equally spaced eigenvalues, in spin-j angular momentum operators and the closely related Sylvester-Kac matrix, and in weakly perturbed diagonal Hamiltonians with well-separated energy levels.

heading: 1 Introduction
text: The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review existing quantum algorithms for computing the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of matrices. Section 3 formally presents the proposed quantum algorithm for spectrum estimation. Finally, Section 4 concludes the paper and discusses potential directions for future research.

heading: 2 Related Work
text: Three major quantum-computing approaches have been employed to address eigenvalue estimation: adiabatic quantum computation, variational quantum algorithms, and quantum phase estimation. In the following, we discuss these approaches, highlighting their respective advantages and challenges.

heading: 2.1 Quantum Adiabatic Computing
text:
Quantum adiabatic computation is a well-established approach for estimating eigenvalues of a sparse Hermitian matrix, based on the quantum adiabatic theorem. Let us briefly review the quantum adiabatic theorem. Assume that H(t) is a time-dependent Hamiltonian of a given quantum system, defined over the interval 0 ≤ t ≤ T, where H(0) and H(T ) denote the initial and final Hamiltonians, respectively. If the system is initially prepared in the ground state of H(0) and H(t) evolves sufficiently slowly, the system will remain in the instantaneous ground state of H(t). The rate of evolution of H(t) must be sufficiently slow relative to the energy gap between the ground state and the first excited state. We now illustrate how the quantum adiabatic theorem can be used to compute the ground-state energy, which corresponds to the minimum eigenvalue of the Hamiltonian. The procedure consists of the following three main steps.

A quantum system is prepared in the known ground state of an initial Hamiltonian H(0). The final Hamiltonian H(T ), or problem Hamiltonian, is constructed such that its ground state encodes the solution to the given problem.

A time-dependent Hamiltonian interpolating between H(0) and H(T ) is defined as

where m: → is a smooth, monotonic function satisfying m(0) = 0 and m(T ) = 1.

Finally, the quantum system is measured after the adiabatic evolution. The measurement yields the ground state of H(T ), which encodes the solution to the given problem.

heading: 2.1 Quantum Adiabatic Computing
text: The correctness of this algorithm follows from the quantum adiabatic theorem. A major limitation of adiabatic state preparation is that the minimum spectral gap can become extremely small as the system size increases, particularly when the initial and final Hamiltonians have substantially different eigenstate structures or when the evolution encounters quantum phase transitions. In such cases, maintaining adiabaticity may require a very long evolution time, making the approach computationally demanding for large systems.

heading: 2.2 Variational Quantum Eigensolver
text:
The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) is a Variational Quantum Algorithm (VQA) widely used for estimating the eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors of a sparse Hermitian matrix. It is a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm that combines a parameterized quantum circuit with classical optimization, where the quantum circuit prepares a trial state and estimates its energy. In contrast, the classical optimizer updates the circuit parameters to minimize the energy. The procedure consists of the following four main components.

An operator: typically a Hamiltonian H that describes a property of the system whose lowest (minimum) eigenvalue we wish to find.

An ansatz: a quantum circuit that prepares a quantum state approximating the eigenvector of interest.

An estimator: a method for estimating the expectation value of the operator H with respect to the current variational quantum state.

A classical optimizer: an algorithm that updates the variational parameters to minimize the cost function.

heading: 2.2 Variational Quantum Eigensolver
text:
A classical optimizer: an algorithm that updates the variational parameters to minimize the cost function.

Although VQE provides an effective framework for estimating eigenvalues and preparing the corresponding eigenstates, its primary objective is typically to determine the ground-state energy (the minimum eigenvalue) and the corresponding eigenstate. The performance of VQE depends on the choice of ansatz, initialization, and classical optimization procedure, and it may be affected by barren plateaus and local minima. Consequently, VQE does not provide a systematic procedure for obtaining the complete spectrum and all corresponding eigenstates of a matrix. In contrast, our work focuses specifically on estimating the complete spectrum and the corresponding eigenstates.

Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) is a quantum algorithm for estimating the eigenvalue (eigenphase) of a given unitary operator. Let U be a unitary operator and |u⟩ an eigenvector of U. The Quantum Phase Estimation algorithm estimates the eigenvalue corresponding to the eigenstate |u⟩. Since U is unitary, all its eigenvalues have unit modulus. Thus,

heading: 2.3 Quantum Phase Estimation Algorithm
text: A key limitation of the standard QPE framework is that it assumes the input state is an eigenstate |u⟩ of the unitary operator U, satisfying U |u⟩ = e2πiλ |u⟩. Consequently, QPE estimates the eigenphase corresponding to a given eigenstate but does not, by itself, provide a procedure for identifying the set of eigenvalues when the eigenvectors are not known in advance. If an arbitrary input state |ϕ⟩ = ∑i ci |ui⟩ is used, where |ui⟩ denotes the eigenvectors of U, QPE returns the eigenphase λi corresponding to |ui⟩ with probability |ci|2. Hence, an eigenvalue whose corresponding eigenvector has zero overlap with |ϕ⟩ cannot be observed. This motivates our approach of using a predefined set of computational basis states as input states across multiple QPE executions. Since every eigenvector has a nonzero overlap with at least one predefined computational basis state, this strategy provides a systematic way to access all eigenvalue-eigenvector pairs without requiring prior knowledge of the eigenvectors.

heading: 2.3 Quantum Phase Estimation Algorithm
text: The idea of applying phase estimation to an input state that is not an eigenstate, so that eigenvalues are sampled according to the overlap of the input with each eigenvector, goes back to Abrams and Lloyd. Our work builds on this idea in three ways: (i) we use a complete orthonormal basis of input states and derive an explicit bound on the number of repetitions needed to recover every distinct eigenvalue with probability at least 1 - δ (Theorem 4); (ii)we give a normalization and phase-recovery procedure that determines the sign of each eigenvalue (Section 3.2); and (iii) we analyze the overall complexity and compare it with classical eigensolvers for sparse matrices (Section 3.5). We are now ready to present our algorithm for determining the spectrum and the corresponding eigenvectors.

heading: 4 Conclusion and Future Directions
text: In this work, we presented a quantum algorithm for determining the spectrum of a sparse Hermitian matrix, including its eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors. For an n × n, s-sparse Hermitian matrix, the proposed algorithm has a runtime of ˜O ( ns2 log 2 (n) ∆min ), where ∆min denotes the minimum spectral gap. Thus, for inverse minimum spectral gaps up to ∆-1 min = O(n), and under the stated sparsity and input-access assumptions, the proposed algorithm achieves an improved asymptotic runtime compared with the O(n3 ) time required by conventional classical algorithms for computing all eigenvalues and eigenvectors of an n × n matrix. This regime includes the Hamiltonians of spin chains engineered for perfect quantum state transfer, as well as spin-j angular momentum operators and the closely related Sylvester-Kac matrix, all of which have equally spaced spectra.

heading: 4 Conclusion and Future Directions
text: Several directions remain for future work. First, replacing the Hamiltonian-simulation subroutine with qubitization-based methods and more efficient phase-estimation schemes could reduce the circuit depth. Second, the requirement of a known lower bound on ∆min could be removed by adaptively increasing the precision, and a rigorous procedure for filtering spurious phase estimates would strengthen the recovery guarantee. Third, we plan to extend the framework to non-Hermitian matrices through efficient Hermitian embeddings. Finally, we intend to validate the algorithm numerically on structured matrices such as the Sylvester-Kac matrix, and to explore applications of spectrum estimation in quantum simulation, the solution of differential equations, and other problems in scientific computing.
